message.content:
### Tenant Rights in Texas (as of 2024) | Area | Key Rights | What It Means for You | |------|------------|-----------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• Must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | Keep a copy of the lease, move‑in inspection sheet, and receipts for any repairs you paid for. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the property in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control).
• Must comply with all local building and health codes. | If something is broken (e.g., a leaky roof, broken heater), you can request repairs in writing. If the landlord fails to act, you may withhold rent or repair and deduct. | | **Repair & Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major issue within a reasonable time, you may **repair it yourself** and deduct the cost from your rent, provided you give written notice and keep receipts. | Keep a detailed log of the problem, the notice you sent, and the repair costs. | | **Rent Increases** | • Landlords can raise rent at the end of a lease term or with proper notice (usually **30 days** for month‑to‑month).
• No “no‑increase” clauses are enforceable. | Review your lease for any notice requirements. | | **Eviction** | • Landlords must provide **written notice** (30 days for nonpayment, 60 days for lease violations, 90 days for no‑cause eviction in month‑to‑month).
• Eviction can only proceed after a court order. | If you receive a notice, you have the right to respond in court. | | **Privacy** | • Landlord must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) before entering the unit, except in emergencies. | Keep a log of any entries. | | **Discrimination** | • Under the **Fair Housing Act** and Texas law, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | If you suspect discrimination, you can file a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **Lease Termination** | • You can terminate a lease early if the landlord breaches the lease (e.g., fails to maintain habitability).
• You may also terminate if the landlord fails to provide required notices or fails to return the security deposit. | Document the breach and give written notice to the landlord. | | **Rent Control** | • Texas has **no statewide rent control** laws. | Rent can increase at the landlord’s discretion, subject to notice requirements. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. If utilities are included, the landlord must maintain them. | Verify utility responsibilities in the lease. | | **Subletting** | • Many leases allow subletting with landlord approval. | Obtain written permission before subletting. | | **Insurance** | • Landlords are not required to provide renter’s insurance, but you are encouraged to obtain it. | Protects your personal property and liability. | | **Legal Remedies** | • If the landlord violates your rights, you can file a claim in **small claims court** (up to $20,000) or pursue a civil action. | Keep all documentation (lease, notices, repair receipts). | #### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read Your Lease** – Understand rent amount, due date, security deposit limits, pet policy, and notice requirements. 2. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, written notices, repair receipts, and communication logs. 3. **Know the Notice Periods** – 30 days for rent increase, 60 days for lease violations, 90 days for no‑cause eviction. 4. **Report Problems Promptly** – Send written notice to the landlord and keep copies. 5. **Keep a Move‑In Inspection Sheet** – Helps with security deposit disputes. 6. **Know Your Local Ordinances** – Some cities have additional tenant protections (e.g., San Antonio’s “Tenant Protection Ordinance”). 7. **Seek Legal Advice if Needed** – Texas tenants’ rights groups, legal aid clinics, or a private attorney. --- **Disclaimer:** This information is general and not legal advice. For specific situations, consult a licensed attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.
